common_name: Rathu Heenati Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Red Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Rathu Heenati is a medium-duration Sri Lankan red-grain landrace flexible enough to grow in either the Yala or Maha monsoon season.

directions: Rathu Heenati is a traditional Sri Lankan rice landrace with slender medium-sized red-bran grains, valued in village agriculture for its adaptability to both of the island's main growing seasons and most of its agroecological zones. Cooked grain is lightly sticky with a mild sweetness, and the variety has long been used in home remedies for digestive upset alongside its place as an everyday staple. Like other traditional lowland rices it is tall-strawed and needs standing water through its vegetative growth, full tropical sun, and a long warm season to fill grain fully. It is sustained today mainly through traditional-rice seed-saving networks rather than large commercial paddies.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
Lakpura — Traditional Rice of Sri Lanka

common_name: Kuruluthuda Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Red Long-Grain Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Kuruluthuda is a long-duration Sri Lankan red long-grain landrace prized for its nutrient-dense bran layer.

directions: Kuruluthuda, whose name references the long slender shape of its red-hulled grain, is a traditional Sri Lankan rice landrace grown for its dense nutritional profile rather than high yield, carrying more protein, fiber, and fatty acids in the bran layer than polished modern rices. Traditional diets recommend it for people managing cholesterol, and it is typically only lightly milled so the colored bran stays on the grain. The plant is long-season and tall-strawed in the manner of pre-Green-Revolution Sri Lankan rices, requiring a standing-water paddy environment and full tropical sun through a long, humid growing season. It survives today mainly through heirloom seed conservation rather than mainstream commercial cultivation.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
Lakpura — Traditional Rice of Sri Lanka

common_name: Madathawalu Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Bold Red Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Madathawalu is one of the fastest-maturing and highest-yielding of Sri Lanka's traditional rice landraces, ready about four months after seeding.

directions: Madathawalu is a traditional Sri Lankan rice landrace carrying bold red grains and grown successfully across nearly every district of the island, a versatility that made it one of the more productive heirloom varieties before modern semi-dwarf rices took over commercial paddies. It reaches harvest faster than many other traditional landraces, filling grain in roughly four months from seeding, which historically made it a reliable staple crop for subsistence farmers. Cultivation follows standard lowland paddy practice: standing water through the vegetative stage, full tropical sun, and warm, humid conditions to finish the crop. It is maintained today chiefly by traditional-rice seed keepers rather than large-scale producers.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
Lakpura — Traditional Rice of Sri Lanka

common_name: Goda Heenati Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Highland Red Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Goda Heenati is a traditional Sri Lankan landrace historically associated with higher-elevation paddies, though it is now grown island-wide except in iron-toxic fields.

directions: Goda Heenati is a traditional Sri Lankan rice landrace with medium, brownish-red grains that farmers once reserved for higher-elevation paddies before its cultivation spread to most of the island, excepting fields troubled by iron toxicity. Its name reflects this highland association, and like other heenati-type landraces it is grown for its distinctive colored bran and traditional-food uses rather than for maximum yield. The plant is long-season and tall-strawed, needing a standing-water paddy, full tropical sun, and a long warm, humid period to mature fully. It persists today mainly in traditional-rice conservation collections and smallholder plots.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
Lakpura — Traditional Rice of Sri Lanka

common_name: Sri Gemunu Cinnamon (High-Yield Ceylon Cinnamon Selection)

planting.note: Establish from vegetatively propagated clonal planting stock in rich, well-drained tropical soil; Sri Gemunu is a high-yield Ceylon cinnamon selection released by Sri Lanka's Department of Export Agriculture, prized for bark with especially high cinnamaldehyde content.

directions: Sri Gemunu is a clonally selected Ceylon cinnamon cultivar released by Sri Lanka's National Cinnamon Research and Training Center to improve on the low bark yield of unselected seedling trees, more than doubling the output of quills per hectare in trials. Its inner bark also tests unusually high in cinnamaldehyde, the compound responsible for cinnamon's characteristic heat and aroma, making peeled quills especially flavorful for culinary and essential-oil use. Grow it as a coppiced tropical shrub-tree in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, cutting stems back periodically to force the thin, tender new shoots from which the best bark is peeled. Outside true tropical climates, maintain it as a large container specimen brought under cover whenever temperatures threaten to drop near freezing.
sources: Department of Export Agriculture, Sri Lanka — cinnamon cultivar release documentation
Seneviratne & Pathirana (eds.), Cinnamon: Botany, Agronomy, Chemistry and Industrial Applications, Springer

common_name: Sri Wijaya Cinnamon (High-Yield Ceylon Cinnamon Selection)

planting.note: Establish from vegetatively propagated clonal planting stock in rich, well-drained tropical soil; Sri Wijaya is a high-yield Ceylon cinnamon selection released alongside Sri Gemunu by Sri Lanka's Department of Export Agriculture.

directions: Sri Wijaya is one of two clonal Ceylon cinnamon selections released by Sri Lanka's National Cinnamon Research and Training Center after decades of clonal selection work beginning in the 1980s, developed specifically to lift bark yields well above those of ordinary seedling-grown trees. Growers who have planted it report sturdier, more uniform shoot production than unselected stock, which translates into more peelable quills per coppice cycle. Cultivation follows standard Ceylon cinnamon practice: full sun, fertile well-drained soil, and regular coppicing to encourage the slender new growth that yields the finest bark. In climates outside the wet tropics, grow it in a large pot that can be sheltered whenever cold threatens.
sources: Department of Export Agriculture, Sri Lanka — cinnamon cultivar release documentation
Seneviratne & Pathirana (eds.), Cinnamon: Botany, Agronomy, Chemistry and Industrial Applications, Springer

common_name: Nortier Rooibos (Commercial Red Bush Tea Selection)

planting.note: Soak hard-coated seed overnight in freshly boiled water, raise seedlings in acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and transplant into full sun; Nortier is the shrub-type, reseeding form selected from Cederberg plantings in the 1930s that underpins nearly all modern commercial rooibos production.

directions: Nortier is the named rooibos type behind most of the commercial red bush tea industry, selected from wild shrub-form, reseeding plants found growing naturally in South Africa's northern Cederberg and developed into reliable field stock starting in the 1930s. Unlike some wild rooibos ecotypes that resprout from a rootstock after fire, the Nortier type regenerates from seed, which suits it to the cultivated field rotations used on modern rooibos farms. Grow it exactly as other rooibos: acidic, sandy, well-drained soil of low fertility, full sun, and minimal irrigation once established, since the plant is adapted to the hot, dry Cederberg summer. Harvest by cutting and bruising young stems, then let the cut material oxidize and dry in the sun to develop the characteristic deep red color and sweet, earthy flavor.
sources: Agricultural Research Council of South Africa
Malgas et al., ecotype and cultivation studies of Aspalathus linearis

common_name: Red Swazi Sorghum (Southern African Heirloom Malting Sorghum)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; Red Swazi is an early-maturing, red-grained Southern African landrace long grown commercially in Zimbabwe for its good malting quality.

directions: Red Swazi is a traditional Southern African grain sorghum landrace named for its uncovered, plump red seed, long favored by Zimbabwean farmers and maltsters for its very early maturity and consistently good malting characteristics compared with longer-season local types. The erect, semi-compact seed heads carry awnless grain that threshes cleanly, and the short growing season lets it fit into drier, shorter-rainfall regions where slower sorghums struggle to finish. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun and manage it like other grain sorghums, with moderate water and minimal inputs once the deep root system is established. Harvest when the grain reaches hard-dough stage for malting or milling into traditional porridge and beer-brewing flours.
sources: SADC/ICRISAT Sorghum and Millet Improvement Program documentation
South African Journal of Plant and Soil — grain sorghum variety release records
